Issued at 255 AM EDT Thu Sep 17 2026

Pattern / Forecast Synopsis: 

Moisture-starved northern stream wave currently zipping eastward 
across the US-Canada border will traverse the region tonight, 
bringing what will likely be a decaying batch of showers. Meanwhile, 
a robust thermal ridge over the southeastern CONUS (contributing to 
record heat in the South) to retrograde westward with time the rest 
of this week, in turn inducing a WNW flow pattern across the Midwest 
and Great Lakes region into this weekend. Stationary front setting 
up shop well to the south, currently remaining the focus for deeper 
moisture and resultant robust convective responses spanning from 
roughly Missouri to eastern Ohio. This particular corridor will 
remain the focus for southern stream wave activity through the 
weekend. 

These waves will likely come in abundance... longwave troughing over 
the Pacific Northwest to draw tropical Pacific shortwaves out of the 
Gulf of California via deep return flow. These waves are set to zip 
through the Four Corners region (where there are already ongoing 
hydrologic issues) and into the central and northern Plains... 
riding the stationary front and associated WNW flow regime through 
the Midwest and into the Great Lakes region. How far north the 
return flow can force a ridge axis and the ejection point of these 
waves will mark the difference between northern Michigan seeing a 
robust period of rainfall or a glancing blow from these systems 
spanning the weekend and into next week.

Details: 

Not a whole lot of change to highlight from previous forecast cycle. 
Aforementioned northern stream wave well within sight, with showers 
blossoming over northern Minnesota and the Wisconsin Highlands, 
zipping east into the western Yoop. Eastward progression of these 
showers to continue through the rest of the night, reaching the 
northwest lower lakeshore and eastern upper after 09z. With hostile 
airmass in place characterized by a complete and utter lack of 
moisture and instability, anticipation is that these already 
diminishing rain showers will decay further as they progress ESE 
through the CWA, with shower activity out of the picture by late 
morning for most. Perhaps a few sprinkles or a light shower lingers 
for our friends in the Saginaw Bay region by early afternoon, but 
should clear by 18z at the latest. 

Rest of the day looks dry as surface high pressure centered over NW 
Ontario intrudes with subsidence aloft and restores meteorological 
order... with peeks of sun likely. Highs top out in the upper 60s to 
mid 70s. Clear conditions tonight with the influence of the surface 
high should lead to another comfortable night with lows in the 40s 
inland and 50s along the immediate lakeshores. Dry weather to 
continue Friday, but as the first of several waves of energy 
approach, anticipation is that clouds increase through the day. At 
this juncture, the big rainfall extravaganza set to manifest just to 
our south as the stationary front fails to lift sufficiently north 
enough to draw rich tropical Pacific moisture into the region... but 
could come close enough to give us fringe impacts. 

Most guidance wants to nose some efficient rainfall into the far 
southern reaches of the CWA Friday night through Saturday... with 
much less prolific rains the farther north one goes. This is echoed 
by the latest WPC Excessive Rainfall Outlooks, which continue to 
pinpoint the southeastern MN / northeast IA through downstate MI / 
northern OH corridor for the greatest rainfall amounts and 
associated impacts. That notwithstanding, current trends depict a 
marked increase in rainfall intensity and frequency the farther 
south one goes from the M-72 corridor... where some guidance members 
are hinting at 1.00-2.00"+ of steady rainfall over that Friday
night - Saturday timeframe... with quickly reducing rainfall 
amounts the farther north one goes. Pattern recognition says 
this probably winds up being a "Manistee Special(TM)", where the
Manistee County area sees the overwhelmingly best shot at the 
aforementioned rainfall amounts, with a sharp gradient of lesser
rainfall to the north / east. Honestly wouldn't be overly shocking
to see little to no rainfall near and north of M-32 if this scenario
manifests. 

Once this initial wave passes by Sunday, guidance is bullish on a 
further southward suppression of the stationary front... which 
should bring us cooler and drier air into next week, with rain 
chances minimal at best and confined to the bottom row or two of 
counties within the APX CWA.
